Let us say my likelihood for a single unit is

Here I marginalized out over all the possible latent states S in order to express the likelihood as a function of the conditional probability of the observed variable Y with respect to the latent state S, and the transition probabilities between the hidden states. To be more precise, I obtain

  int<lower=1> n;   
  int<lower=1> n_tot;            
  int<lower=1> k;                
  int<lower=1> s;                 // number of states of the HMM

parts:
Hi Giorgio,

This is what the generated quantities block is for, but as a first step get the model working without worrying about outputing the states.  Once you have
that you can add a generated quantities block to produce the states using your estimated parameters.  The key point is that HMC doesn't sample from discrete
parameters so they need to be simulated separately. 

Krzysztof

messages.author: 6ad178c9bfa534b7
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: HMM: estimation of Hidden States
parts:
Here's an HMM in Stan that is slightly extended from the one in the : https://github.com/jrnold/ssmodels-in-stan/blob/master/stan/hmm.stan It uses the forward algorithm to marginalize of the latent states in the model, and then backward samples the latent states. It also calculates the backward probabilities, state probabilities and global decoding (Viterbi) in the generated quantities block. 

Also, it's worth noting that when you marginalize over the states and sample the states in the generated quantities step, I think it is partially collapsed Gibbs sampler (https://wwwf.imperial.ac.uk/~dvandyk/Research/09-jcgs-pcg.pdf) and thus you are getting a sample from the posterior distribution. I've found this method of marginalizing over latent states in the model block and sampling them in the generated quantities also works very well / samples more efficiently in the case of linear dynamic models.

You want to use bernoulli_logit (or bernoulli_logit_log to call it
as a function) --- then you won't need an explicit inv_logit() transform.

You want to tighten your priors to something more reasonable for what
you expect output to be --- those normal(0,100) are probably way too wide,
which means they can't guide sampling.

You want to move anything that just involves data to the transformed
data block (e.g., rep_vector(0,s)). And move anything you don't need for
the log likelihood to the generated quantities block (don't know if that's
anything).

You want to vectorize these if possible:

> for (j in 1:s){
> m[T_act,j] <- inv_logit(alpha[j] + X[T_act] * col(gamma,j));
> diag_pag[T_act,j] <- poisson_log(N[T_act], lambda[T_act,j]);
> diag_prob[T_act,j] <- bernoulli_log(C[T_act], m[T_act,j]);
> }

You almost certainly don't want to be creating diagonal matrices if you can
at all avoid it as it adds to the autodiff overhead.

Applying exp() is bad news --- it's expensive and tends to be unstable.
Try to use algebra to get rid of explicit exp() if at all possible. For
example, those q variables are defined in terms of exp and then have log
applied to them.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] HMM: estimation of Hidden States
parts:
> On Apr 2, 2015, at 8:35 PM, Giorgio Paulon <giorgio...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Bob, that was a great help! Now my code is running much faster.
>
> I do have a couple of questions, though:
>
> (1) I found the overflow issue: the critical line is
>
> lambda[T_act] <- exp(eta' + X[T_act] * tau);
>
> The calculation is much faster witout the exponentiation. However, a lot of warnings are raised because lambda is the parameter of a Poisson and, if a do not transformate lambda on a positive support, it can take negative values.
> X is a matrix with non negative integers. However, I do not want to constrain the parameters eta and tau to a positive support, as they could take negative values. How can I avoid the problem of negative values of lambda (constraining the transformed
> parameter lambda on a positive support does not work)?

You need to do something to keep those parameters positive.
But rather than writing

lamba <- exp(gamma);
y ~ poisson(lambda);

use

y ~ poisson_log(lambda);

The _log takes the parameter on the log scale.

Or if you use functions, it's poisson_log_log() for the parameter on
the log scale version. Sorry the notation's so confusing. Adding
the _log was a bad decision I made very early on and haven't wanted
to change for fear of messing up everyone's existing models.

You want to make sure the support of the log probability function
defined by the model matches the constraints declared on any
parameters.
> (2) Can the poisson_log and the bernoulli_logit_log functions be vectorized as their corresponding sampling statements?

The sampling statement

y ~ foo(theta);

is roughly shorthand for

increment_log_prob(foo_log(y,theta));

The difference is that the former drops constants.

So the foo_log() form will return a single value, which is
the sum of the probability function outputs if there are vector
inputs.

- Bob
